For nearly two years, student protesters demanded a fundamental transformation of Serbia’s political system, and the Oct. 25 elections marked an extraordinary step toward achieving it. Their movement defeated the formidable political machine of longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in a stunning upset.

The Student List secured approximately 53 percent of the vote and 140 parliamentary seats, with a record voter turnout of nearly 70 percent. It ended 14 years of uninterrupted rule by Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which is left with 103 seats. A new government must be formed within 90 days of the official results.

For nearly two years, student protesters demanded a fundamental transformation of Serbia’s political system, and the Oct. 25 elections marked an extraordinary step toward achieving it. Their movement defeated the formidable political machine of longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in a stunning upset.

The Student List secured approximately 53 percent of the vote and 140 parliamentary seats, with a record voter turnout of nearly 70 percent. It ended 14 years of uninterrupted rule by Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which is left with 103 seats. A new government must be formed within 90 days of the official results.

The victory is remarkable not least because the students disregarded almost every convention of electoral politics. They rejected traditional parties, eschewed recognizable leadership, and offered voters something closer to a moral crusade than a normal political program. The elections therefore functioned less as a choice between competing platforms and more as a referendum on Vucic’s years in power.

Winning power and exercising it are different things. The qualities that made the student movement effective in opposition—from the students’ status as political outsiders to their ideological heterogeneity—could become liabilities in government. Now, the Student List must prove to an expectant public that it can move beyond deliberating what needs to change and govern.

Serbia’s ongoing political upheaval traces back to November 2024, when a concrete canopy collapsed outside the newly renovated Novi Sad railway station, killing 16 people. Initial demonstrations demanded government accountability for the disaster and transparency over who was responsible for the construction and how public funds were spent.

As protests spread across Serbia, the disaster became a symbol of broader anger over endemic corruption, political patronage, and the ruling party’s stranglehold on state institutions. The movement evolved into a campaign for wholesale political change, culminating in snap parliamentary elections. Students, who carried out university occupations and demonstrations that put immense pressure on Vucic’s government, were the driving force.

The students’ grassroots efforts had structural advantages. The movement was decentralized, operating through network-based university groups that made it difficult for the government to identify leaders it could discredit or co-opt. The students also rejected Serbia’s opposition establishment, whose chronic infighting, electoral failures, and tainted reputation made it an unappealing alternative to Vucic. This helped the movement attract support from across the political spectrum.

The students initially insisted their objective was to compel Serbia’s institutions to function better rather than to enter electoral politics. But after six months of protest, they began to recognize the limitations of their approach. At the time, I argued in Foreign Policy that street demonstrations alone would not transform Serbia, and that the students would have to turn to the ballot box to achieve lasting change. In May 2025, they took that step, demanding snap elections.

Vucic resisted calls for an early vote for another 16 months before finally dissolving parliament on Sept. 9 and scheduling the October elections. He resigned as president to contest the election as the SNS candidate for prime minister, temporarily handing the position to parliamentary speaker Ana Brnabic. (Serbia must hold an early presidential election by Dec. 27.)

So, the students did enter politics—though on unique and even inadvisable terms. Rather than joining forces with established parties, they assembled the Student List, an electoral coalition that included academics, professionals, and political newcomers. Candidates were nominated and vetted by student plenums at individual university faculties, which agreed on a final list through a nationwide process of collective decision-making.

The Student List retained a horizontal structure and avoided elevating a charismatic leader, consciously rejecting the political culture that Vucic cultivated. That strategy was an enormous gamble. The students bet that public dissatisfaction was widespread enough to bring habitual nonvoters to the polls: primarily politically disengaged Serbians, first-time voters, and people who had become disillusioned with electoral politics in the Vucic era.

But they did not have an obvious plan for winning over the government’s supporters, many of whom had a material stake in Vucic’s patronage system. SNS reportedly has more than 700,000 members; party loyalty is often a prerequisite for securing public-sector employment. In smaller towns where the state is a major employer, supporting the ruling party is therefore as much a matter of economic self-preservation as political conviction.

While in power, the SNS cultivated and invested in preserving the status quo, which included public-sector employees, business owners benefiting from state contracts, and older voters who credited Vucic with rising pensions and economic stability.

Vucic campaigned on his economic record and sought to discredit the student movement, accusing its supporters of attempting a so-called color revolution and portraying their slate of inexperienced candidates as a threat. His message was familiar: The SNS delivered stability, infrastructure investment, and higher wages, pensions, and living standards. Serbia has experienced genuine economic development under Vucic, but as elsewhere, the rising cost of living has strained household finances.

By contrast, the student movement asked voters to embrace uncertainty for the promise of a better future. Its 11-point reform agenda promised to restore the rule of law and respect for the constitution, free the judiciary from political interference, confiscate illegally acquired wealth, and dismantle the patronage networks that have permeated state institutions.

The SNS campaign rested on what it thought was a straightforward calculation: Would voters risk their livelihoods on an inexperienced opposition promising to tear down the existing order? This underestimated how much public tolerance for Vucic had deteriorated. His party is plagued by allegations of corruption, cronyism, and abuses of authority; the touted stability increasingly appeared to serve a small elite.

Vucic’s government also overestimated its traditional methods of intimidation. International election observers documented voter pressure, misuse of state resources, and unequal campaign conditions. Pro-government forces dominated airtime and broadcast overwhelmingly negative coverage of the Student List, according to the European Center for Research, Transparency, and Accountability. These tactics still failed to prevent the opposition from large-scale mobilization.

Ultimately, the Student List won the public’s vote, with its perceived weaknesses serving as strengths. By rejecting the established opposition, it avoided inheriting the baggage of politicians who had repeatedly failed in challenging Vucic. Its lack of obvious ideological identity united voters with otherwise incompatible convictions, and its refusal to appoint a dominant leader deprived the government of an obvious individual to demonize.

The victory of the Student List bears comparison with that of Prime Minister Peter Magyar in neighboring Hungary’s elections in April. Both movements capitalized on exhaustion with entrenched governments that blurred the distinction between party and state and turned discontent with corruption into a broader rejection of the political order.

But there is an important difference. Magyar—a former member of longtime Prime Minister Viktor Orban’s party—offered Hungary a recognizable alternative built around his leadership, combining institutional accountability with a message about deteriorating public services and living standards. Serbia’s student movement offered something more radical: an opportunity to replace the political culture itself.

The question now is whether a movement assembled around opposition to one leader can develop the coherence necessary to govern without him. The Student List’s parliamentary majority should allow it to form a government without coalition partners. But the movement has yet to settle elementary questions of leadership, including who will become prime minister and how to reconcile ideologically diverse factions.

Ilija Srdanovic, a physician and professor who became the lead candidate on the electoral list, confirmed that government appointments will be decided collectively by lawmakers, while the student plenums that elected them intend to retain an oversight role. But this risks creating competing centers of authority—a tension that is already surfacing. The Student List lawmakers and the plenums are currently deliberating how to balance the grassroots participation that defined the movement with the elected representatives’ practical need to make decisions quickly.

The Student List also encompasses left-wing academics, liberal reformers, and conservative nationalists whose different positions on key foreign-policy issues that have long been political third rails in Serbia—such as Kosovo’s independence, support for Russia, and Serbia’s European integration—could prove especially difficult to reconcile in government.

Another immediate challenge is the presidential election that is due by the end of next month. The Student List must put forward a credible candidate while simultaneously forming a government. Defeat could leave it sharing power with a hostile president, further complicating its ambitious reform plans. The scale of the October upset makes a student victory likely, however. Those who voted for the Student List likely won’t want a president who throws sand in the gears of the parliament they mobilized to elect.

The new leadership will face enormous practical obstacles to governance. SNS loyalists remain embedded throughout the state bureaucracy, where they could obstruct reforms and frustrate corruption investigations that the new government intends to pursue. Particularly challenging will be reforming the police and intelligence services, whose senior officials have been accused of surveilling and intimidating government opponents, as well as links to organized crime.

Dismantling these networks requires more than moral conviction. It demands administrative competence, political discipline, and the ability to distinguish legitimate reform from politically motivated retribution. This last distinction is particularly important. The new government will face intense pressure to deliver accountability for years of alleged abuses, and the Student List has already called on judges and prosecutors to either pursue corruption cases or resign. But indiscriminately purging the state apparatus risks the sort of politicization that the students promised to end.

Equally, the new leadership cannot neglect Serbians’ material concerns. A government devoted to prosecuting its predecessor while failing to improve ordinary lives might find that enthusiasm for political renewal has a limited shelf life. Concerns are emerging about the Student List’s vague economic program, with economists questioning its investment plans. An approaching budget deadline will quickly test the new government’s economic credibility.

It would also be foolish to write Vucic off. The SNS retains 103 parliamentary seats, extensive patronage networks, and influence over local administrations and media outlets. Vucic has already vowed to return to power, though he must first keep his political machine intact. Vucic has been involved in national politics since 1993; he spent 12 years in opposition after the fall of Slobodan Milosevic in 2000. He will not simply disappear.

Dismantling an entrenched political system is one thing, but building a functioning alternative is another. The students have won an impressive mandate, but their sweeping ambitions will take more than one parliamentary term. They must learn not only how to win elections but also how to retain voters’ confidence. That demands a transition from protest to politics, from moral absolutism to compromise, and from opposition to responsibility.

Serbia’s student movement accomplished something that many people believed impossible: They ended an era of political dominance through the ballot box. Now, their task is to demonstrate that they can build something better in its place.

Aleks Eror is a journalist and political consultant from Belgrade. His work has been published by the Financial Times, UnHerd, and other publications. X: @slandr

#6014. Democrats Shouldn’t Squander Their Chance to Launch a Foreign Policy Revolution

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

MATTHEW DUSS is Executive Vice President of the Center for International Policy. From 2017 to 2022, he served as Chief Foreign Policy Adviser to Senator Bernie Sanders.

The Imperative of Ambition in a New Congress

Tuesday’s election made clear that endless wars, political corruption, and the high cost of living are three of the American public’s top concerns. They are deeply interrelated—and the new Congress must address all three. That will require a true foreign policy revolution that grapples not just with the outrages and failures of the Trump administration’s foreign policy but also with the ways in which past Democratic or Democrat-supported foreign policies have contributed to today’s crisis. There will be a temptation among some Democratic leaders, in Congress and beyond, to limit the scope or pace of change. But to find a way out of today’s crisis and move beyond the failures that have afflicted American foreign policy for the past several decades, Democrats will need to have the courage to face a hard truth: that President Donald Trump’s abuses of power and unilateral warmaking are not so much a break from Washington’s militarist mindset as they are a particularly aggressive, predatory expression of it.

The incoming Democratic majority will face a national security environment in which the most severe challenges to U.S. safety and prosperity come from within. That’s why Congress should shut down the Iran war immediately but also recognize that it can make the United States more secure only if it pairs a foreign policy shift with a frontal assault on spiraling costs and political corruption. Political polarization; government corruption and dysfunction; increasing dominance of political and economic life by a small handful of mercurial oligarchs; and a president who recklessly and unilaterally launches unauthorized military interventions while relentlessly seeking opportunities to enrich himself, his family, and his cronies—all pose more immediate danger to the safety and prosperity of the American people than does any foreign enemy.

When Democrats take control of Congress in January, they will have considerable power to challenge the corruption and malfeasance of the Trump administration. Control of committees and of the congressional calendar will provide the opportunity for sorely needed oversight. But although the Trump administration deserves aggressive investigation, Democrats must aim higher—and use the opportunity to articulate a genuinely compelling alternative for American foreign policy.

The first and most urgent task will be ending the Iran war, a reckless and unpopular conflict that has become even less popular as Americans have felt its effects on their wallets. Congress must respond to widespread bipartisan anger among voters at Trump’s war and abuse of war powers by using all the tools it has, especially its power to cut funding. It has been encouraging to see Democrats continuing to oppose any supplemental budget request by the administration for the war. It is an area where Democrats have gotten tripped up in the past when they’ve been afraid of accusations that they don’t “support the troops” if they oppose funding for foolish, counterproductive wars. With Democrats having held firm against any additional funding for the war, those days appear to be gone. That is good.

But Democrats need to go further. They should be prepared to oppose all funding for the military, including blocking votes on the National Defense Authorization Act, the annual bill setting out the broad scope and budget for the Defense Department, in order to put an end to hostilities in Iran. In fact, not only should they be willing to withhold funding from the Pentagon, but they should also be willing to withhold funding for the entire government, and threaten another government shutdown if the bill does not prohibit any funding for Trump’s war. December 11 is the deadline for a continuing resolution to keep the government funded and operating. If ever there was a reason for Democrats to threaten to withhold their votes, stopping a blatantly illegal and globally destructive war that American voters have now resoundingly rebuked is it.

Democrats must also be willing to take a hard look at the continuity between Trump’s use of military violence and past uses of force by administrations of both parties, and the bipartisan support for that violence. The groundwork for the Iran war was laid by the Biden administration’s unstinting support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza (as even some former administration officials have acknowledged), but also by years of U.S. refusal to impose any consequences on the Israeli government despite clear evidence of ongoing violations of human rights and international law. Trump’s strikes on alleged “narcoterrorist” drug boats in the Caribbean represent the logical evolution of long-standing treatment of the United States’ drug problem as a “war,” and of casually applying the label of “terrorist” to justify any and all measures, including execution without due process. Seeking accountability for these abuses will require acknowledging the past complicity of both Republicans and Democrats.

Democrats must also take on corruption, a key node connecting the country’s domestic and foreign policy crises. In doing so, they will be walking through an open door. Polls consistently show that political corruption is high on Americans’ list of concerns. According to a recent Harris poll conducted for The Guardian, “Nearly nine out of 10 Americans said that government corruption, as defined as elected officials putting their own or their donors’ financial interests ahead of the public’s, is a problem.” A mid-October CNBC All-America Economic Survey found that voters are more concerned about government corruption than any other issue, including high grocery and gas prices. In September, Gallup reported that “Americans’ perceptions of government corruption in the U.S. are at their highest level in 20 years, with 89% of U.S. adults saying it is widespread.”

To say that the Trump administration provides a target-rich environment for a strong anticorruption push is to commit felony understatement. Exposing foreign gifts to Trump and conflicts of interest by family members, contracts awarded to Trump’s oligarch donors and new tech buddies, and the selling of pardons, as well as restoring enforcement of the Corporate Transparency Act, the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, and related task forces, should all be part of the plan. Democrats should drill down into Trump’s wildly corrupt “Board of Peace” for Gaza, which U.S. Representative Jamie Raskin, the Maryland Democrat set to chair the House Judiciary Committee, rightly referred to as a “global slush fund.” The obvious conflicts of interests of Trump’s diplomatic envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner also demand investigation.

The good news is that effective anticorruption does not necessarily require new legislation; it merely requires that existing legislation be enforced. An August 2025 essay in Foreign Affairs, co-authored with my colleagues Casey Michel and Trevor Sutton, laid out a more expansive case for Democrats putting anticorruption at the center of their foreign policy platform. (A recent essay by Casey Michel lays out a more detailed agenda for the new Congress.)

Ultimately, the most important step toward tackling corruption will be reforming the campaign finance system. The United States is an outlier among developed democracies in that its system of campaign finance allows for what is essentially legalized bribery. Legislators speak openly about campaign contributors expecting “returns on investment” for their political donations. This is an outrage. In recent years, foreign actors have increasingly begun bankrolling American legislators, taking advantage of massive loopholes in campaign finance laws and the Federal Election Commission’s lack of enforcement.

Confronting this will be no small task. At a minimum, Congress must move to legislate a response to the Supreme Court’s 2010 Citizens United decision, which effectively greenlighted bottomless campaign funding from American corporations. It must also reform the Federal Election Commission, providing the body with much-needed resources to investigate campaign finance crimes and restoring the practice of allowing congressional appointments to the commission, which has become little more than an appendage of the executive branch.

All of the above steps must be connected to the top concern among American voters at this moment—the high cost of living. Democrats have disagreements in several policy areas, particularly in foreign policy. Their coalition is diverse. But there is consensus around addressing Americans’ material needs urgently and aggressively. Such an approach would confront Trump’s reckless use of tariffs (while recognizing that the neoliberal taboo on tariffs is a thing of the past), rising gas prices because of the Iran war, the need to restore the global minimum tax, the threat of job losses to AI, and the increased power of tech oligarchs over Americans’ economic and political lives, including on foreign policy, as Elon Musk’s restriction of Ukraine’s Starlink connection demonstrated. The approach should involve a mix of tactics, including hearings, oversight investigations, and legislative proposals.

Many of these efforts may not produce new laws in the next two years. But they could become the backbone of a winning agenda for Congress and for a Democratic administration in 2029. Most important, they would represent a step toward the forging of a new American political consensus on which a new and durable foreign policy can be built.

#6013. Van Hollen announces bid for majority leader, but Schumer says he has the votes

Sen. Chris Van Hollen announced Thursday night that he would run for Senate majority leader, launching a challenge to Sen. Charles E. Schumer of New York, the current Democratic leader.

Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat first elected to the Senate in 2016, served in leadership in the House and has been chairman of both the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. He has said since the midterm elections he was listening to fellow Senate Democrats about the possibility of a run for the top job.

“In this election, the American people called for change. They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people,” Van Hollen said in a statement. “It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership. This is not about any one person – it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”

Schumer has already said he has the votes needed to continue serving as the leader.

“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader. I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people,” Schumer said in a statement.

Schumer’s supporters were quick to highlight the success at the ballot box in 2026, with the Democratic caucus potentially growing to 56 seats if former Rep. Mary Peltola prevails in Alaska.

“Chuck has outlined an aggressive plan for the new Democratic majority which is directly responsive to the message we heard from the voters, and he has the experience and unique mastery of the Senate process to make it happen,” Sen. Angus King, a Maine independent who caucuses with the Democrats, said in a statement. “Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?”

In keeping with the World Series theme, Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., echoed King with her own statement of support for Schumer.

“The Brewers just had a record season, and next year is not the time to change our management,” Baldwin said. “The same is true in the Senate.”

In an interview with MS NOW about his run, Van Hollen conceded that Schumer would be the favorite in the secret-ballot contest, which will take place in December.

“Am I the underdog? Yes,” Van Hollen said. “You’re talking about an incumbent who uses the power of incumbency to, you know, provide deals to people.”

Van Hollen outlined legislative priorities including restoring Medicaid funding that Republicans cut in last year’s budget reconciliation law and extending Affordable Care Act tax credits. But he suggested Democrats need to go further.

“We need to extend tax credits for the Affordable Care Act, but we can’t stop there, right? We have a completely broken health care system. It’s become profits, not people. And so my view is, we also need in the first 100 days to make health care more affordable for tens of millions of people,” Van Hollen said. “We need to immediately make it clear that nobody’s going to pay one penny to subsidize data centers. … We need to make sure that we have a livable minimum wage.”

He also said he would not take sides in contested Democratic primaries, and he would make sure the DSCC did not take money from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC.

Van Hollen’s early backers include progressive Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who emerged from a hotly contested Democratic primary in Michigan while the Senate Democratic political apparatus was backing Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich.

“In April, I was the first candidate in the country to call on Senator Chris Van Hollen to lead Senate Democrats, and I am proud to stand with him in his bid to become Senate Majority Leader,” El-Sayed said in a statement. “Michiganders demand money out of politics, money in pockets, and Medicare for All. Sen. Chris Van Hollen offers both the courage to go toe-to-toe with the Trump administration to deliver for working people and the experience to maneuver the Senate caucus. It’s why he has my full support to lead our caucus.”

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

The highlights this week: Tanzania’s opposition leader is sentenced to prison, the African National Congress suffers historic losses in South Africa’s local elections, and the Ethiopia-Sudan rift deepens.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

The highlights this week: Tanzania’s opposition leader is sentenced to prison, the African National Congress suffers historic losses in South Africa’s local elections, and the Ethiopia-Sudan rift deepens.

One year after Tanzania’s disputed October 2025 presidential election, the country remains in a political crisis. Incumbent President Samia Suluhu Hassan ran largely uncontested, winning 98 percent of the vote after the country’s electoral body disqualified her main opponents. Her second term began with a deadly crackdown on protesters by state security forces that saw more than 1,000 people killed, according to rights groups.

Since before the elections, prominent opposition figures have been charged with treason, allegations that they strongly reject. Among them is Tundu Lissu, the leader of opposition party Chadema, whom authorities blocked from running against Hassan last year. On Friday, Lissu was sentenced to four years in prison for “incitement” but acquitted of treason.

“History will record how the court searched for a lesser charge simply to keep me in prison,” read a post published by Lissu’s team on his X account after the verdict. Fellow Chadema party member John Pambalu was charged with treason last month.

Following Lissu’s verdict, Chadema on Sunday accused police of holding 10 of its leaders and members for “prolonged periods” without bringing them before a court, alleging torture and forced confessions. Rights groups, including Amnesty International, labeled Lissu’s trial “a deeply flawed process” and called on Tanzania’s government to “end the misuse of treason” and other laws to silence government critics.

Tanzanian activists report a continuous wave of state-sponsored intimidation and abductions since last year’s election, allegations that the government denies. In July, authorities arrested more than 130 people over planned anti-government demonstrations—before they took place. The government had banned political rallies the previous month.

“Young people are wandering around with no place where they feel they can speak out. When they do speak, they face intimidation. They are threatened and told they could disappear, be abducted, or face various other forms of harassment,” said Gasper Kagonda, a prominent Tanzanian content creator, at a July conference on the country’s political landscape. Much of Kagonda’s TikTok channel is devoted to anti-corruption activism.

One year on from the post-election violence, Tanzanians are no closer to accountability. Even casualty figures are still in dispute: In April, a government-appointed commission of inquiry said that it documented at least 518 deaths and more than 2,000 injuries during the unrest, a fraction of the numbers estimated by rights groups. The commission also placed most of the blame on protesters.

The government withheld its full report from the public, drawing criticism from Amnesty International and the United Nations Human Rights Office. Hassan then ordered a second commission of inquiry in August that is still underway. Critics say that both commissions have failed to engage with victims’ families.

“There has been no justice or accountability for the hundreds of victims of enforced disappearances, extrajudicial killings, arbitrary arrests and those subjected to torture and other cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment,” wrote a group of U.N. experts last month.

Tanzania’s weakened opposition continues to resist Hassan’s growing authoritarianism through legal appeals and underground movements. But with her mandate secured through 2030, it is unlikely that she will face major domestic opposition during the remainder of her term.

The international community is unlikely to speak out, either: Amid new discoveries of natural gas deposits in Tanzania, foreign powers appear to be prioritizing critical minerals investment and energy security over human rights.

A U.S. government-backed consortium is negotiating an agreement to invest more than $500 million in a nickel mining project in Tanzania. The Tanzanian government is also nearing a previously stalled $42 billion gas deal with Norwegian energy firm Equinor and British energy giant Shell. U.S. multinational ExxonMobil also has stakes in the project.

These investments are mistakes, argued Kenneth Mohammed in the Guardian. “The world cannot celebrate Africa’s economic rise while ignoring the blood staining the streets,” he wrote last year. “Tanzania’s tragedy is not an isolated event—it reflects the broader struggle for democracy across the continent.”

Thursday, Nov. 12: Ghanaian Finance Minister Cassiel Ato Forson presents the country’s 2027 budget.

The U.N. Security Council renews its mandate for the U.N. Multidimensional Integrated Stabilization Mission in the Central African Republic.

Sunday, Nov. 15: Cape Verde holds presidential elections.

Africa at COP31. This year’s U.N. climate change conference, known as COP31, began this week in the Turkish city of Antalya amid global heat waves, floods, and droughts.

Africa is the source of just 4 percent of global carbon emissions, despite being home to 17 percent of the world’s population. Yet the continent faces an outsized impact from climate change. Deadly wildfires ravaged forests across Algeria, Morocco, and Tunisia earlier this year, while seasonal floods displaced thousands of people in Nigeria and Ghana.

Led by Ghana, African countries are negotiating as a unified front at COP31. As the world’s biggest historical fossil fuel polluters backtrack on their previous emissions targets and commitments to mobilize $300 billion annually on climate finance for developing countries by 2035, African nations have focused on securing equitable climate finance.

The African bloc wants to ensure that countries meet their previous financial commitments, especially to the Green Climate Fund, which helps finance climate resilience and green energy access projects in developing countries.

Next year, the U.N. climate summit moves to Africa, with Ethiopia due to host COP32.

South Africa’s election. The African National Congress (ANC) won less than 31 percent of the overall vote in local elections held last Wednesday in South Africa. It was the party’s worst result ever and a further sign that the country’s political landscape is fragmenting.

The ANC’s main rival—the largely white-led and pro-business Democratic Alliance (DA)—gained nearly 25 percent of votes. Former President Jacob Zuma’s far-left party uMkhonto weSizwe came third, with about 10 percent.

As predicted in last week’s newsletter, in many cities, no party won a majority. In Johannesburg—where the DA won nearly 35 percent of the vote to the ANC’s 20 percent—leaders will now need to decide on a coalition government that may include different combinations of the ANC; DA; and a smaller party, the center-right ActionSA, which came third in the city with 16 percent of the vote.

U.S.-Congo peace deal. The Democratic Republic of the Congo has urged the ‌United States to deliver investments promised under a peace-for-minerals deal after the joint steering committee overseeing the countries’ strategic minerals partnership met in Paris last week.

The United States brokered a peace deal between Congo and Rwanda in 2025 that granted U.S. companies “exclusive” mineral extraction rights in Congo. “Our requirement is to move from signed agreements to real investments,” Congolese Economy Minister Daniel Mukoko Samba said on Thursday

Congo wants the partnership to focus on local mineral processing and ending the conflict in the country’s eastern region. Congo has increased its copper exports to the United States since the deal was signed. But U.S. companies have faced legal hurdles in implementing the agreement from Chinese and European organizations, which have voiced concerns over international law.

Also at issue: The deal has not been approved by Congo’s parliament. And it has sparked complaints over its suspension of informal artisanal mining in the country.

Ethiopia-Sudan rift. Ethiopia and Sudan expelled each other’s diplomats and closed their consulates last Wednesday, the latest episode in an escalating spat between the two neighbors.

Sudan accuses Ethiopia of backing the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary group fighting Sudan’s military in the country’s civil war. Ethiopia accuses Sudan and its allies, Egypt and Eritrea, of backing rebels in its Tigray province. (During the height of the 2020-2022 Tigray civil war, Sudanese troops moved into the border area, leading to localized clashes with Ethiopian forces.) All countries deny the accusations.

Meanwhile, Sudan’s de facto military government filed a formal complaint with the U.N. Security Council and the African Union last week accusing Ethiopia of allowing the RSF to launch devastating drone attacks from its territory. The risk of a proxy war in the Horn of Africa is growing.

Historic appointment. Morocco’s King Mohammed VI appointed Fatima Ezzahra Mansouri as the country’s first female prime minister in September after her party won general elections earlier that month. In Foreign Policy, Ilhem Rachidi argues that while Mansouri may have limited powers compared to the king, her new role is still symbolically important.

“If she succeeds in shaping policies that improve Moroccans’ lives and support gender equality, she may very well leave her mark on a country that is striving to modernize even as it has long leaned conservative,” Rachidi writes.

UNESCO bids. In the South China Morning Post, Jevans Nyabiage reports that Beijing is providing financial backing and technical training to help African nations combat underrepresentation on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

African sites account for just 9 percent of UNESCO’s 1,273 total locations, while Europe and Asia are home to the vast majority of global listings. China’s initiative is anchored by a $1 million fund established by Quanzhou municipal authorities in March 2025, which supports nomination dossiers and conservation capacity-building across the continent.

Nosmot Gbadamosi is a multimedia journalist and the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Africa Brief. She has reported on human rights, the environment, and sustainable development from across the African continent. X: @nosmotg

#6008. A Recipe for Disaster in Taiwan

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

REBECCA LISSNER is Senior Fellow for U.S. Foreign Policy and Director of the Future of American Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations. She served as Deputy Assistant to the President and Principal Deputy National Security Adviser to the Vice President during the Biden administration.

MIRA RAPP-HOOPER is a Visiting Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution. She was Special Assistant to the President and Senior Director for East Asia and Oceania and Director for Indo-Pacific Strategy at the U.S. National Security Council during the Biden administration.

Just a few years ago, U.S. President Joe Biden caused a stir when he confirmed publicly that his administration would defend Taiwan if the island were attacked by China—a divergence from the traditional U.S. policy of strategic ambiguity, in which Washington does not commit to taking any particular action. In May, U.S. President Donald Trump made waves for taking a different position. In a television interview, he described Taiwan as “a very good negotiating chip” in dealings with Beijing and mused that the island was close to China but far from the United States, implying that U.S. interests in Taiwan were negligible. In doing so, Trump seemed to confirm something many Asia watchers had feared: that this U.S. president would be willing to loosen the United States’ commitment to Taiwan to bolster his relationship with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

A few days later, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee that there had been no change in U.S. policy toward Taiwan. But Trump’s words were alarming nonetheless—in part because they reflect a shift in Washington that goes beyond the Oval Office. Since 2025, politicians from both parties have been shying away from affirming the United States’ long-standing support for Taiwan. Meanwhile, China is developing new strategies to coerce Taiwan without going to war, and Beijing will be increasingly tempted to use them if it judges that the U.S. commitment to Taiwan is waning among both politicians and the public.

Yet that would be a grave miscalculation on China’s part. In fact, the United States’ interests in Taiwan are growing, not diminishing. Whatever the nature of Washington’s rhetoric right now, the United States would have to respond to any action by Beijing that threatened those interests, and both countries would then face a great-power crisis. To defuse this dangerous situation, American leaders must update the United States’ Taiwan strategy to reflect a new reality—and they should begin immediately.

Taiwan’s unique international status has long made U.S. policy complex. The Republic of China, now known as Taiwan, was a World War II ally of the United States. When the People’s Republic of China was founded on the mainland, in 1949, the Republic of China’s president, Chiang Kai-shek, decamped to Taiwan, and the United States maintained formal diplomatic ties with Chiang’s government, not the People’s Republic of China. In 1954, as the Cold War crested in the Pacific, the United States concluded a formal mutual defense treaty with Taiwan, in part to forestall increasingly aggressive artillery barrages from the mainland. Nearly 20 years later, however, when U.S. President Richard Nixon and his national security adviser, Henry Kissinger, began to engineer a diplomatic opening to the government in Beijing, they knew it would cost Taiwan.

In part because they understood that building diplomatic ties with Beijing would be painful for Taiwan and cause controversy in Congress, where Taipei had many boosters, Nixon and Kissinger slow-walked the process. So did Nixon’s successor, President Gerald Ford. It finally fell to President Jimmy Carter to make the change. On January 1, 1979, the United States ended its alliance with Taiwan and recognized the mainland government as “the sole legal Government of China.” Congress was irate. Lawmakers from both parties quickly drafted the 1979 Taiwan Relations Act, which remains in force. The law requires Washington to provide Taipei with defensive arms, creating the trappings of an alliance with Taiwan despite the relationship’s unofficial status. In 1982, the Reagan administration made an additional set of commitments to Taiwan, known as the Six Assurances. These include an affirmation that Washington does not endorse Beijing’s sovereignty claims over Taiwan and a promise that the United States would not use arms sales to Taiwan as a bargaining chip.

In the 50 years since, U.S. Taiwan policy has been remarkably successful. Through its partnership and arms sales, the United States has helped underwrite peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait, and Taiwan has thrived as a democracy and an economy, even as Washington has maintained a relationship with Beijing. But U.S. commitments to Taiwan have lately come under increasing strain. China has proceeded with a massive military buildup designed to give Beijing the option to take Taiwan by force; used coercive economic tactics, launched cyberattacks, and interfered in elections to put pressure on Taipei; and run frequent army and coast guard exercises to demonstrate its ability to strangle the island. All of this has stoked concerns across the Pacific that the United States’ long-standing partnership might not be enough to keep the peace in the Taiwan Strait.

The fear that China could attempt to retake Taiwan by force, possibly during Xi’s tenure, has grown in recent years. Analysts have frequently cited 2027 as the beginning of the window of maximum danger, based on a 2021 statement made by Philip Davidson, the former commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, about when the People’s Liberation Army might be prepared for an invasion. But this timeline was never hard and fast, and Xi’s recent purge of more than 100 officers has likely delayed the military’s readiness. U.S. intelligence assessments do not anticipate an invasion of Taiwan next year, and most scholars believe the Chinese government would consider such a move as a last resort only if unification could not be accomplished by other means.

The primary danger now is that Xi will escalate a pressure campaign designed to coerce Taiwan into negotiating a change in its status. Since 2025, China’s leaders have used their diplomatic channels to the Trump administration, including Xi’s direct line to Trump, to insist on American concessions on Taiwan in exchange for progress in trade talks. In May, China secured a pause on a planned $14 billion U.S. arms sale and other defense funding for Taiwan. Beijing may hope that additional incremental moves will further weaken Taiwanese confidence in the United States and that such actions will be difficult for Trump or a future U.S. president to reverse.

China is also clearly planning for more dramatic forms of coercion. It has a few options: since 2022, China’s military has practiced blockades of Taiwan, and its coast guard has simulated a quarantine of the island’s major ports. Beijing could also use customs enforcement or other administrative measures to attempt to assert its jurisdiction over Taiwan while minimizing the likelihood that the United States would intervene to stop it. If Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te, who favors Taiwanese independence but has not pursued it in office, is reelected in 2028 and Chinese leaders believe that the path to a peaceful unification is closing, Xi may consider using these tools against the island in late 2028 or early 2029, before a new U.S. administration takes office. Given Trump’s alienation of U.S. allies in Asia and Europe and Washington’s limited means to respond to a maritime quarantine, Beijing might hope to get away with such a large-scale coercion campaign without inviting serious pushback.

Taiwan’s growing strategic importance makes Beijing’s development of new coercive options more concerning. Washington is no longer maintaining a partnership with Taipei because of a historical commitment or, as Beijing would have the world believe, to needle China. The artificial intelligence boom has put Taiwan at the center of the global economy. Taiwan is a critical supplier for the U.S. tech industry, and the United States recognizes that it cannot be a leader in AI without Taiwan.

The scale of the United States’ economic dependence on Taiwan is revealing. Taiwan is the country’s fifth-largest trading partner; a Chinese blockade of the island would imperil more than $250 billion in trade and could shave more than three percent off U.S. GDP in a year, according to a Bloomberg report. As much as 97 percent of the global supply of the high-end logic chips used in smartphones and other advanced electronics are produced or packaged in Taiwan. Losing access to Taiwanese chips could reduce advanced electronics production globally by 60 percent, with factories forced to rely on their chip inventories. The United States’ auto and medical device industries could deplete their inventories in a matter of weeks. The U.S. firms Amazon, Apple, and Nvidia are among the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company’s ten largest customers, which together represent more than $14 trillion in market capitalization. With AI growth buoying the U.S. stock market and the broader economy, a crisis in Taiwan would trigger a crash—potentially one similar in scale to the stock market crash at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.

The economic effects of a Chinese effort to squeeze Taiwan would not be limited to the United States. The research firm Rhodium Group has conservatively estimated that a yearlong blockade of the island could cost the global economy between $2 trillion and $3 trillion. A full-scale war would be far worse; Bloomberg has estimated that it would cause $10 trillion in economic losses and a global recession. It is therefore increasingly likely that the United States would be forced to act if Taiwan’s supply chains were put in jeopardy. The cost of standing aside would simply be too high.

Yet just when the United States needs to be doing all it can to prevent a crisis, Washington’s support for Taiwan appears to be wobbling. Trump’s musings about Taiwan’s geographical distance from the United States and his use of arms sales as a bargaining chip are the headline examples, but they are not the only indicators of a shaky U.S. commitment. Policy analysts have argued that the United States should change its position to definitively oppose Taiwanese independence or even withdraw U.S. forces from the military bases in Japan and the Philippines that are closest to Taiwan.

Public opinion in the United States is shifting, too. Americans’ feelings toward China have warmed considerably over the past two years, according to a July 2026 Chicago Council on Global Affairs survey. A majority, 57 percent, support friendly cooperation and engagement with China, whereas 40 percent support an active effort to limit the growth of China’s power. The share of Americans who see China’s territorial ambitions as “a critical threat” has decreased by more than ten percentage points since 2022, and those who favor the use of U.S. troops if China invaded Taiwan has fallen from 52 percent to just 38 percent.

In part, the declining support for defending Taiwan reflects Americans’ growing wariness of instability and conflict. A sense that the world was descending into chaos helped fuel Trump’s 2024 campaign; as president, Trump has heightened that sense by taking assertive military action in places such as Iran and Venezuela. Americans are now suffering the economic consequences of nine months of war in the Middle East, further deepening antiwar sentiment, as the midterm election results vividly demonstrate. Candidates for office used to clamor to sound tough on China, but many now blanch at the idea of suggesting that the U.S. military should defend Taiwan against a Chinese invasion, calculating that this is not the time to be seen as a hawk.

Of course, public attitudes can change quickly during a crisis. If China actually committed aggression against Taiwan, Americans could become more supportive of a strong U.S. response. And if the early stages of a conflict saw American casualties or a Chinese attack on U.S. critical infrastructure, the U.S. public could very well rally around the flag and demand a muscular intervention.

For now, however, China may believe that the United States’ will and ability to fight are both diminishing. The war with Iran has substantially reduced U.S. military readiness for a Taiwan contingency. The United States has used up much of its missile defense stock, including roughly two-thirds of its Patriot interceptor inventory, which was already depleted by U.S. aid to Ukraine, and as much as 80 percent of THAAD interceptors against Iranian drones and missiles. Even before the Iran war, analysts had warned that the U.S. military could run out of long-range, precision-guided munitions in a fight over Taiwan; now, the munitions shortfalls have become perilously acute. The war has also drawn military assets away from the Indo-Pacific. In August, Washington moved its last aircraft carrier in Asia, the USS George Washington, out of the region. It has also relocated missile defense systems to the Middle East, including Patriot and THAAD systems that had been deployed in South Korea.

The result is an increased risk of dangerous miscalculation. Should Chinese leaders assess that the United States’ commitment to Taiwan is wavering in both political parties and that the country is ill prepared for a fight, they might conclude that they have an opportunity to pressure Taiwan without inviting an American response. Yet because the United States has a greater interest in Taiwan today than at any point in history, Beijing’s bet could turn out to be wrong. China could announce a maritime quarantine of Taiwan or another coercive measure only to have the United States intervene, potentially prompting a great-power standoff.

Avoiding such a showdown will require American leaders to recommit to deterrence. First, Washington needs to update the way it communicates its positions. In their public remarks, policymakers should clearly state that the U.S. economy’s dependence on Taiwanese exports makes peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait a vital interest of the United States. American political leaders should emphasize to Beijing that the United States has an obligation to prevent a crisis that would tank the U.S. stock market, cut critical supply chains, and fell many American industries.

Clarifying U.S. interests would not impugn 50 years of careful diplomacy with China, nor would it require any change to U.S. policy as established by the Taiwan Relations Act, the Six Assurances, or the series of joint U.S.-Chinese statements, made between 1972 and 1982, known as the Three Communiqués. The updated statements, rather, would convey to Chinese leaders that certain changes to the cross-strait status quo would be unacceptable to the United States, even if Taiwan were to acquiesce to those changes under pressure. Washington would support a peaceful unification, for example, only if the process guaranteed the security of critical supply chains.

Once the United States makes its interests clear, it will also have to back up its statements with a new playbook to deter Chinese actions that fall below the military threshold. Beijing may already be in the early stages of imposing a quarantine on the island. Washington should not tolerate additional measures that interfere with commerce and maritime traffic in and out of Taiwan. To deter China from taking such steps, the next U.S. Congress should use legislation to clarify its wholesale, bipartisan opposition to Chinese blockades, quarantines, and other restrictions. Even if the White House continued to take a softer position, this would send a message to Beijing that other political actors might force the president’s hand. Congress should also press the administration to prepare punitive diplomatic and financial measures for use in the event of an escalating Chinese quarantine of Taiwan. By planning these reprisals well ahead of any coercive action, Washington would signal that a maritime pressure campaign would entail clear costs for Beijing and carry dangerous escalation risks.

The United States should strengthen military deterrence, too. The next Congress must pressure the Trump administration to release the stalled $14 billion package of arms sales to Taiwan, as well as other security assistance the administration is slow-rolling. Congress has a legal obligation to do so under the Taiwan Relations Act. Pausing security aid violates U.S. policy, and allowing the Trump team to make this concession in its likely quixotic pursuit of rapprochement with Xi only weakens Washington’s hand.

Washington does not have to—and shouldn’t—take these steps alone. U.S. allies such as Germany, Japan, and South Korea would suffer nearly as much as the United States if China were to take control of Taiwan’s semiconductor industry. These countries have an interest in working quietly together to deter and develop joint responses to Chinese coercion while also collaborating to diversify their chip supply chains and make them more resilient. In the United States, this work does not have to wait for a new presidential administration. Congress can send delegations and use other diplomatic opportunities to start developing plans with parliamentary counterparts abroad.

As the 2028 U.S. presidential election approaches, moreover, candidates from both parties should speak clearly about the country’s strong economic interests in Taiwan and about their commitment to deterrence. This does not require embracing bellicose positions, but presidential candidates do need to state firmly that any move by Beijing to choke off vital supply chains would harm U.S. interests and demand an American response. Consistent messaging would also signal to China’s leaders that they should not expect a future administration to be bound by Trump’s policy concessions—and signal to allies that come 2029, the United States will again be a reliable partner in standing up to China’s economic aggression.

The United States needs to update its Taiwan policy, but ceding ground as Trump has done only makes the cross-strait balance less stable. Unlike other Cold War–era policies, the importance of preventing Chinese aggression against Taiwan has become more—not less—vital with the passage of time. U.S. interests in Taiwan are plainer and easier to explain than they have ever been. Only by stating those interests clearly and backing up the words with actions can the United States continue to avert a crisis or conflict that would be devastating for all.

#6007. UN renews Iran's committee seat amid war with US, sparking backlash: 'Morally bankrupt'

Hillel Neuer, executive director of UN Watch, says Iran's renewed committee seat illustrates how the UN can lend legitimacy to governments accused of serious human rights abuses.

The United Nations reconfirmed Iran to its seat on the Committee for Programme and Coordination on Wednesday, sparking outrage from member states who believe the country’s record of aggression should disqualify its representatives from the committee’s work to review human rights, women’s rights and counterterrorism programs.

Ahead of the vote, Hillel Neuer, executive director of UN Watch, a human rights watchdog, said he believes the move gives Iran another tool for the regime’s propaganda machine.

"They use it," Neuer said. "You'll see a headline in Iranian propaganda right away: ‘Hey, look, we were elected to yet another body.' And it sends a signal… As they're killing their own people, what does the world have to say?"

Neuer believes Iran’s continued spot on the committee gives Tehran a nod of international legitimacy amid its ongoing conflict with the U.S., showcasing the U.N.’s uneven record for creating a forum to deter international violence.

ISRAEL ACCUSES UN OF PLACING IT ON SAME SEXUAL VIOLENCE BLACKLIST AS HAMAS TERRORISTS, SEVERS TIES

Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian speaks as he holds a picture of Ali Khamenei, former supreme leader, during the 81st General Assembly at the United Nations in New York, Sept. 23, 2026. (Timothy A. Clary/AFP via Getty Images)

"Sometimes [the U.N.] is effective. Sometimes they’re not. Sometimes, even when they’re effective, they’re effective in a bad way. There’s an effect, but it’s to empower dictatorships," Neuer said.

"The U.N. spends a lot of its time attacking democracies like America, like Israel. America gets condemned every year for the embargo in Cuba. Last year, there was one resolution on Iran, one on North Korea, one on Myanmar — and 15 on Israel. And Hamas, Islam and jihad were never mentioned once. That happens a lot at the U.N."

Iran was reconfirmed with the support of 144 ballots cast by the U.N. General Assembly.

The Committee for Programme and Coordination consists of 34 member states, each of which is elected to the body for a three-year term. Although it is not one of the U.N.’s six main committees, it reviews the organization’s plans and priorities, making recommendations on their design, priorities, coordination and effectiveness.

Iran’s renewal to the post prompted an outcry from lawmakers in the U.S. on Tuesday afternoon.

"The United Nations elected Iran — the world’s biggest exporter of terrorism — to the committee responsible for establishing priorities on disarmament, counterterrorism and women’s rights," the House Foreign Affairs Committee wrote in a statement posted to X.

FREED AMERICAN REVEALS BRUTAL IRAN PRISON ORDEAL, WARNS HOSTAGES FACE GREATER DANGER

Flags wave outside the United Nations in Manhattan. (Stephen J. Boitano/LightRocket via Getty Images)

"The United Nations is morally bankrupt: no sane person can take it seriously."

Similarly, Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand issued her own statement condemning the move.

"Canada is steadfastly opposed to giving Iran a seat on the UN Committee for Programme and Coordination — and Canada voted against Iran’s inclusion today at the UN. The committee should be comprised of countries entrusted with shaping the work of the United Nations and must uphold the principles of its Charter. The Iranian regime silences dissent at home and fuels instability across the Middle East. We stand with the people of Iran," Anand said.

Notably, Australia also joined the opposition, voting alongside Canada against Iran’s confirmation.

"Australia strongly opposes Iran’s nomination to the UN Committee for Programme and Coordination and voted against. Iran’s human rights violations and destabilizing conduct undermine multilateralism," Foreign Minister Penny Wong wrote.

Neuer believes it's not just Western countries that will be watching how the U.N. treats Iran. He noted that aggressors constantly monitor the international field to get a sense of how it might react in the future.

"It's like Putin looks when Obama said we 'have a red line in Syria. Use chemical weapons — red line.' Well, Syria used chemical weapons. And Obama... did nothing. That sent a message. Shortly thereafter, Putin invaded Ukraine. I'm not saying that invasions are gonna happen the next day, but these things send messages, and constantly governments are taking the temperature. What is the pushback?" Neuer said.

He also observed that although many in the U.S. view the U.N. with some skepticism, other countries still use the group as a barometer of international consensus.

"The United Nations is considered for many a repository of international legitimacy; it may not be so in the United States… but in many parts of the world it is regarded as the arbiter of international legitimacy," Neuer said.

IRAN IS NOT A NORMAL NATION YOU CAN MAKE DEALS WITH; IT’S A NATIONAL SECURITY THREAT

In a protest against the regime in Iran on March 7, 2026, in Washington, D.C., Iranian American women march with their hair uncovered, refusing strict edits of Iran that force women to cover their hair. (Fox News Digital)

"What is the signal you're giving to the ayatollah regime? They murdered tens of thousands of people. They're hanging dissidents. They are torturing women who defend their right not to cover every piece of their hair. They beat political prisoners. What message does the world have to send? Did you give them a pat on the back? Or did you? Did you penalize them?"

#6006. Calls for Nvidia probes, new chip export limits intensify

The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday did little to quell bipartisan demands from Congress for an accounting of potential national security fallout from his affair with an alleged Chinese spy and talk of adding tougher chip export controls to the annual defense authorization bill.

Huang admitted on Sunday to having an affair, and reports say that it was with Alice Huang, an executive at Singaporean tech company and Nvidia customer Megaspeed, whom the U.S. government believes spied for China, according to recent reports. The New York Times and Reuters reported he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters Thursday that he supports the Senate investigating Huang’s potential influence on U.S. artificial intelligence and chip policy.

“I think that it would make sense because of the… nature of the association… and the governments and the national security interests we were talking about here,” Thune said, though he said he thought it would be “wrong” to make assumptions about how close Huang’s relationship with President Donald Trump has been.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., echoed the need for lawmakers to delve into the scandal, saying in a post on X that “Congress must demand answers.”

“The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Were government officials told not to investigate because of Trump’s relationship with Mr. Huang? What did Trump know when he personally invited Mr. Huang aboard Air Force One?” Schumer wrote, referring to the president having invited Huang to accompany him to China in May.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said at a press conference that Reps. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., and Jim Himes, D-Conn., the ranking members of the Foreign Affairs and Intelligence committees, respectively, are leading Democrats’ efforts to “get to the bottom of what has happened.”

“We need a classified briefing made available to members of Congress as it relates to the Nvidia situation,” Jeffries said. “And to the extent that our national security has been compromised, the American people deserve answers, and we’re going to work to make sure that happens.”

The investigations look likely to begin before control of Congress changes hands in January.

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., who chairs the House select China committee, told reporters that his panel, along with House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence, are in negotiations with Huang to find a date for his testimony before Congress.

“The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” Moolenaar said. “What ways is Chinese intelligence influencing his perspective, his perspective influencing national security policy?”

Last week, the chairs of the three committees sent a letter to Huang requesting that he appear at a joint closed-door briefing. Moolenaar said that if Huang does not agree to a date, the committees will subpoena him.

Late Thursday, he joined with House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., and House Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark., in sending a new letter to Huang seeking a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 1. They also wrote to Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter seeking a similar interview on Dec. 2. Separately, Mast wrote to Jeffrey Kessler, the Commerce Department undersecretary for industry and security, seeking his appearance at a committee hearing on Dec. 3.

Moolenaar also said that Congress needs to understand what privileged information Chinese intelligence may have gained access to through Huang and how they may have tried to influence U.S. policy.

“We need to have strong safeguards when it comes to our technology and export controls,” Moolenaar said. “And [Huang has] been one of the strongest proponents for not having export controls. This shines a whole new light on that discussion.”

A proposed manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill (S 4784) contains several possibilities for those safeguards, including requirements for chip security mechanisms that would allow for verification if semiconductors are diverted to countries of concern and a ban on exporting certain very powerful chips to those countries. The House NDAA does not contain similar language.

However, House Armed Services Chair Mike D. Rogers, D-Ala., is open to the restrictions. He told reporters Wednesday that he “would like to see” semiconductor export controls in the NDAA, but that the Huang scandal had not changed his position.

Democratic Caucus Vice Chair Ted Lieu, D-Calif., told reporters on Thursday that after reports that the federal government had been aware of Huang’s affair with the alleged spy, the administration should have shared the information with Congress.

“The administration needs to be investigated for hiding this information from Congress and the American people,” he said.

Lieu also suggested that Nvidia’s reported donation to the White House ballroom project influenced the Trump administration’s decision to allow the export of some powerful Nvidia chips to China.

“There is no reason to do that. That hurts our national security, and we have an opportunity right now to fix that in the upcoming National Defense Authorization,” Lieu said.

Mast said the Huang revelations could give new momentum to including chip export rules in the NDAA. He also said that his “directive” on the issue came “straight from the admin” and informed his objectives on the committee.

“Don’t let chips be smuggled to China. Make sure that American companies get to buy them first,” Mast said. “Make sure that the machines that make them don’t get sold to them, even though it’s the Dutch that make the machines. Make sure that they can’t access it remotely.”

Mast’s committee has advanced many of those priorities, including some of the language included in the NDAA.

In March, the committee on a unanimous vote advanced legislation known as the Chip Security Act, which would require chip security mechanisms to verify that certain semiconductors subject to export controls aren’t diverted to countries of concern, including China and Iran.

The committee also advanced bills to require the Bureau of Industry and Security and the State Department to work with allied suppliers of semiconductor manufacturing equipment to implement export controls to prevent the equipment from going to countries of concern, and to require licenses for the export of certain powerful chips, including banning exporting certain chips to countries of concern.

Versions of all three bills are included in the Senate manager’s amendment to the NDAA.

The scandal has also led to calls for oversight of the Commerce Department, including Secretary Howard Lutnick, for its handling of export policy and actions around Huang.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters Thursday that Lutnick and Nvidia should testify “before Democrats can set the narrative.”

“If there is some reasonable basis or some way to discount some of the reporting, the best way to do it is request a meeting with us and give us a briefing,” Tillis said. “Because otherwise, you’re going to get what you get in an oversight hearing in about six weeks.”

Asked about oversight of the Commerce Department’s role in the Huang scandal, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, who chairs the Commerce Committee, said his panel “has engaged in vigorous oversight under Republican presidents and Democrat presidents and will continue to be [engaged in it].”

On Wednesday, prior to Huang’s resignation, Senate Banking ranking member Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller requesting that they “preserve all documents, communications, records, and other materials regarding the export of NVIDIA’s advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China.”

“This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,” the senators wrote.

In a statement Thursday, Warren said that Huang’s resignation did not “absolve” him of the need to answer questions. She also called for the passage of stricter export controls, including the bill to ban the export of certain chips to China.

Sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., sent his own letter on Wednesday to Lutnick, Rubio, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, requesting an update on the Justice Department’s investigation into Megaspeed for possibly diverting U.S. chips to China.

Savannah Behrmann, John M. Donnelly, Jacob Fulton and David Jordan contributed to this report.
